title: This Year's El Niño Is Breaking Records, and It May Grow Stronger
summary:
Scientists say the El Niño that formed this year is already the most intense ever recorded, based on daily ocean temperatures. And it probably has not reached its peak yet.

An El Niño is a natural climate pattern. It forms in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean near the equator, the imaginary line around the middle of Earth. During an El Niño, the ocean there becomes warmer than normal and releases huge amounts of heat into the air. That can affect weather around the world, bringing droughts, floods, heat waves and strong storms.

By September 21, the sea surface where El Niños form was 3.08 degrees Celsius (5.54 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the average from 1991 to 2020. "It has been a remarkable event," said Nathaniel Johnson, a climate scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA. He expects this El Niño to peak "within the next few months."

NOAA has not officially called it a record yet. That is because NOAA now uses a newer way to measure El Niños. By that measure, the El Niño of 1997 and 1998 is still stronger. But NOAA's own forecast suggests that record could soon be broken too.

Johnson said this year has already brought a quieter Atlantic hurricane season, a busier Pacific hurricane season and droughts in Central America. By late fall, the southern United States may get more rain, while the Pacific Northwest may be drier than normal.

Scientists are still debating how climate change affects El Niño. Climate scientist Nathan Lenssen said Earth's warming has put more energy into the oceans.

El Niños usually last about a year. After a big one, the opposite pattern, called La Niña, often follows.
why_it_matters: A record El Niño can shift rain, storms and temperatures around the world, including in the United States, and scientists are still working out how a warming planet changes these patterns.

keywords.explanation: A climate pattern is a repeating change in ocean and air conditions that affects weather over months or years.
The equator is the imaginary line around the middle of Earth, halfway between the North and South Poles.
Droughts are long periods with much less rain than normal.
The peak is the highest or strongest point something reaches.
La Niña is the opposite of El Niño, when the same part of the Pacific becomes cooler than normal.
The Pacific Northwest is the region of the United States that includes Washington and Oregon.

background_read: El Niño and La Niña are two opposite phases of a natural back-and-forth pattern in the tropical Pacific Ocean.
Normally, winds push warm surface water toward the western Pacific, but during an El Niño those winds weaken and warm water spreads east along the equator.
Because the Pacific is so huge, that extra warm water releases enough heat to shift rain, storms and temperatures in many parts of the world.
Scientists track El Niño by measuring sea-surface temperatures and comparing them with long-term averages.
